claims.text: The corrosion susceptibility of pre-exposure Q235 steel is governed by heterogeneity in its native passive oxide layer.
Electropolishing can remove superficial inhomogeneities and promote formation of a uniform passive oxide film on Q235 steel.
A uniform passive oxide film will suppress localized corrosion and pitting relative to untreated Q235 steel.
Pre-exposure Q235 steel has inherent microstructural inhomogeneities.
Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a native, non-uniform passive oxide layer.
Passive-film uniformity and integrity mediate the formation of localized galvanic cells and the onset of pitting.
A uniform passive oxide film minimizes localized differences in electrochemical potential.
Minimizing localized electrochemical-potential differences reduces micro-galvanic-cell formation at grain boundaries and inclusions.
Suppressing local anodic sites prevents rapid initiation of pitting corrosion.
Elevated temperature accelerates anodic reactions in the specified chloride environment.
Accelerated anodic kinetics at elevated temperature increase the protective importance of a homogeneous passive layer.
Electropolished Q235 steel will have higher charge-transfer resistance than untreated Q235 steel.
Electropolished Q235 steel will have lower pit density than untreated Q235 steel.
Electropolished Q235 steel will undergo less mass loss than untreated Q235 steel.
The corrosion-performance differences between electropolished and untreated Q235 steel will be more pronounced at approximately 80°C than at approximately 25°C.
The controlled comparison will use 3.5 wt.% NaCl at approximately 25°C and 80°C without applied mechanical stress.
Treatment uniformity, oxide-layer characteristics, and environmental interactions may influence the degree of corrosion suppression.
Failure of electropolished specimens to show statistically significant improvements in charge-transfer resistance, pit density, and mass loss at both temperatures will falsify the hypothesis.
